Test Principles... List Variables...
There's no way I'd simply trust that person's instincts.
After all, probabilities are the true guidelines for Dolls.
Five Dolls have been sent to the designated location per your request.
What are you looking for in this control group?
Bernoulli's experiment plus Markov's process.
...I see. Setting up "Maze Cage No. 2" as a blank control group.
Five civilian Dolls, no goal, no instructions, not even a requirement.
We're like abandoned military dogs, aren't we?
Stop using your boring animal trainer analogies.
Though, I do wonder what the enemies in Miss Persica's experiments look like...
Eight-armed robots, perhaps.
What if it's a six-eyed elf bishoujo?
...My guess is that they're enemies that the AR Team has encountered before.
Hah? Why is your answer so matter-of-fact and boring? You took a peek at the answer, didn't you?
Indeed. Since we waited outside for a bit, I checked the adjacent training ground, and the subjects there were of AR Team.
You just know that the top students will always bring back with them new exercises from the teacher.
And who are the Dolls in the other training ground?
Griffin Dolls, just like us.
Oh, I know who they are! Very generous of you to call them like that.
If the perfect grade is 100 and AR Team can get a 90, then we'll score something around 60. And there's no way the Rifle Team on the other side gets more than a 30!
You're wrong.
Hah?
If this is an easy, entry-level test, then the AR Team will get 100, we can score a 60, and RFs 30.
However, if we're talking about a hard test, AR still gets its perfect score, but both us and the RFs aren't making it past the 20 mark.
...What do you mean?
It means that the best will always be the best, but there isn't a bottom limit for how poorly you can do.
We need to work very hard just to stay in the middle of the pack.
Then what are we waiting for! Let's get started—
